title: The fourth and fifth ways
hookLine: degrees of goodness and order in nature; thinkers still argue about these

cards: An arrow leaves the bow and crosses the whole field into the center of the target. The arrow knows nothing. It doesn't aim.
It doesn't want the bullseye. And yet, from a good archer's hand, it gets there. That arrow is Thomas Aquinas's own picture, the last image in his five ways.
Two are left. Today, walk them, then ask what an argument like this is for. Today's word: the fourth and fifth ways.

teach.h: MORE AND LESS NEED A MOST.
teach.b: The fourth way starts from more and less. We call one act kinder than another, one answer truer, one life nobler. Thomas says more and less only make sense measured against a most.
So there is something truest, best, noblest, and so most fully being, which causes the being and goodness in everything else. This, he says, we call God.
His example shows his age: fire, the hottest thing, causing heat in all the rest. That's the science he learned. The point he's after is goodness, not fire.
The fifth way is the arrow. Things without minds still act for an end. An acorn heads for oak.
Rain falls, plants turn toward light, regularly, not by luck. But a thing with no mind can't head for a goal unless someone with a mind directs it, as the archer directs the arrow.
So there is someone intelligent who directs natural things to their ends. This, he says, we call God.

teach.h: MINDLESS THINGS ACT FOR AN END.
teach.b: Notice what it's not: it isn't about how intricate a thing is, but how reliably mindless things lean toward a goal.
The Psalm sings the same direction, in the Douay-Rheims: "The heavens shew forth the glory of God."

teach.h: A WAY HAS TO BE WALKED.
teach.b: Now the arguing. Thomas meant these as real arguments, and readers, believing and not, still push on them: on the step from more to most, on whether nature's regularity needs a director.

teach.h: THE HEAVENS SHEW FORTH THE GLORY OF GOD.
teach.b: But Thomas called them ways. A way doesn't drag you. You walk it, weigh each step, and decide.
He wrote them for beginners, in a book that states the other side first. An argument, for him, is an invitation to think, not a fist.

how: In Catholic classrooms the five ways are often taught as a set, with time given to the objections raised against them and to Thomas's own replies.

games.q: what does “the fourth and fifth ways” mean?
o: the last two of the seven sacraments of the Church
arguments from degrees of good and from nature's aim
two rules for fasting before Holy Communion

games.q: the fourth and fifth ways — tap the pairs.
p: more and less need a most
mindless things act for an end
directs the arrow to its mark

s: the fifth way is about how intricate living things are
it's about things without minds reliably acting for an end, like an arrow sent to its mark.
Thomas's example in the fourth way is fire as the hottest thing
an example from the science he learned; the point he's after is goodness and being.
Thomas meant the five ways as idle guesses
he meant them as real arguments, and he called them ways: paths a person has to walk and weigh.

games.q: a friend tells you the fifth way doesn't convince them. what fits Thomas's own way of working?
o: tell them they just aren't thinking clearly.
state their objection fairly, then give your reply.
drop the subject and never raise it again.
games.why: the Summa puts the objections first and answers each one. even in the article on the five ways, Thomas states the case against God's existence before he replies.

practice: Choose an argument you disagree with, about God or anything that matters, and walk it step by step, asking at each one whether it holds for you, until you find the exact step where you get off.
Don't argue back; just notice that the argument can't make you do anything, only invite. If you pray, ask for an honest mind; if you don't, simply look at the spot where you stepped off.

wordCard.voice: The fourth and fifth ways. Thomas's arguments from degrees of goodness, which point to a most, and from order in nature, which points to a mind that directs.

orig.note: Latin: in five ways — Thomas writes that God's existence can be shown in five ways.

carryVoice: Your line: arguments invite, not force. A way has to be walked. See you tomorrow.
